en: Record of the Monk Huisheng’s Mission to the Western Regions during the Northern Wei Dynasty.

In the eleventh month of winter, in the first year of the Shenguī era of the Wei, the Empress Dowager dispatched the bhikṣu Huisheng of Chongli Temple, together with Song Yun, a native of Dunhuang, to the Western Regions to retrieve Buddhist scriptures. In total, they obtained one hundred and seven [volumes].
These ten works are all sublime Mahāyāna scriptures.
He first set out from the capital.
After traveling west for forty days,
they reached Mount Chiling,
which is the western frontier of the kingdom.
The mountains were devoid of grasses and trees;
there were birds and mice that shared the same burrows.
Traveling westward again for twenty days,
he reached the kingdom of Tuyuhun. From there,
he traveled another three thousand five hundred li to the west.
Upon reaching the city of Shanshan,
he traveled west again for one thousand six hundred li to reach the city of Qiemo.
There are statues of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas made during the time of Lu Guang’s subjugation of the Hu.
Furthermore, traveling westward for one thousand three hundred and seventy-five li,
one arrives at the city of Mo.
Traveling twenty-two li further to the west,
one arrives at the city of Hanfeng,
where there is a stupa built by the people of Khotan to enshrine offerings for the Buddha.
Beside it were several thousand small stupas,
with tens of thousands of banners suspended from them.
Traveling further west for eight hundred and seventy-eight *li*, one arrives [at the next site].
Upon reaching the kingdom of Khotan,
there was a covered stupa (stūpa) built by a former king,
as well as the sandals of a Pratyekabuddha.
It has not decayed to this day.
The territory of Khotan extends three thousand li from east to west.
On the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Shenguī era.
He entered the kingdom of Jukhupa.
Its people dwell in the mountains and do not practice slaughter.
They eat the flesh of animals that have died of natural causes.
Their customs and language are the same as those of Khotan.
Their literature is identical to that of the Brahmans.
The boundaries of their country can be traversed in five days.
In the eighth month, he entered the borders of the kingdom of Khotan (Kebantuo).
Traveling westward for six hundred li,
he ascended Mount Congling (Pamir).
Traveling west again for three days,
he arrived at the city of Patamaṅga.
After another three days, he reached the Pool of the Poisonous Dragon.
In the past, King Bāṇa used a Brahmin’s incantation to curse them;
the dragons then moved westward beyond the Pamir Mountains,
more than two thousand li from this place.
Setting out from the Congling Mountains,
he ascended step by step for four days until he reached the pass.
According to the intermediate and inferior reckonings,
it is actually half a day’s journey from the kingdom of Khotan.
It is the kingdom of Kapisa.
It is situated on a mountain peak.
From the Pamir Mountains to the west,
all waters flow westward into the Western Sea.
The people of the world say that this is the center of heaven and earth,
occurring in the middle of the ninth lunar month.
He entered the country of Bāhlika.
High mountains and deep valleys;
the perilous paths were as they had always been.
They have built their cities along the mountains;
they wear felt garments and dwell in caves,
where humans and livestock depend upon one another.
The wind and snow were biting and intense.
There was a great Snowy Mountain,
which from afar resembled a peak of jade.
In the early part of the tenth month, he entered the country of the Hephthalites.
They have no walled cities or fortifications and dwell wherever water and grass are found.
They do not know written characters.
Their years do not exceed [the standard length].
Twelve *zhou* months constitute one year.
He received tributes from various kingdoms;
to the south as far as Drela,
and to the north reaching the limits of the Chelü.
To the east it reached Khotan;
to the west it extended as far as Persia,
encompassing more than forty kingdoms.
All [the neighboring states] come to pay tribute;
it is the most powerful among them.
The king’s tent measures forty paces in circumference.
Their utensils were made of the seven treasures;
they did not believe in the Buddha-dharma,
and they killed living beings for blood-based offerings.
Seeing the Wei envoy prostrate and receive the imperial decree,
[the mission] traveled more than twenty thousand li from the capital.
In the eleventh month, they entered the kingdom of Persia.
The territory is extremely narrow;
it takes seven months to traverse.
The inhabitants dwell among the mountains and valleys.
The snow shone brilliantly like the sun.
In the middle of the eleventh month, he entered the kingdom of Śāmbī and gradually emerged from the Pamir Mountains.
The rocky peaks were steep and perilous;
men and horses could only just pass through.
Iron chains were suspended for crossing.
Its bottom could not be seen from below.
In the first decade of the twelfth month, he entered the kingdom of Wuchang,
which borders the Pamir Mountains to the north.
To the south it connects with India;
the climate is mild and warm,
and the plains and fields are lush and fertile.
The people and their resources were abundant;
the king maintained a vegetarian diet and observed perpetual fasting,
worshipping the Buddha morning and night.
After midday, he began to attend to the affairs of state;
the sound of the bells then resounded throughout the world.
He made offerings of various flowers.
Upon hearing that a Wei envoy had arrived,
he prostrated himself and received the imperial decree.
Within the kingdom is the place where the Tathāgata dried his robes and sandals upon a stone;
other traces of the Buddha’s footsteps are found throughout, each one vividly manifest.
He frequently visited temples and stupas, treading upon them.
The bhikṣu’s observance of the precepts was pure and austere.
In the middle of the fourth month of the first year of the Zhengguang era, he entered the kingdom of Gandhāra.
The territory is similar to that of the country of Wu-chang.
Its original name was Yebaluo (Yavala).
It was subsequently destroyed by the Hephthalites.
He then established Cheluo as king.
All the people within the kingdom were Brahmins.
They serve as scribes for the Hephthalites;
however, the king is fond of killing and does not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
They contended with Kaśmīra over their borders,
fighting for successive years;
thus the army grew weary and the people were resentful.
He sat and received the imperial decree with arrogance and insolence, showing no respect;
he sent the messenger to a single monastery.
Provisions were extremely meager.
Traveling westward, they reached the great river Sindhu;
traveling further west for thirteen days more, they arrived.
He arrived at the city of Bhuṣāvatī.
Its walls were straight and well-proportioned,
and its groves and springs were lush and flourishing.
The soil abounds in rare treasures,
and the customs are pure and virtuous.
Eminent monks and sages possess extraordinary spiritual attainments and lofty conduct.
The stone image is magnificent,
its entire body gilded with gold leaf.
There is also a footprint of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Traveling westward for another day,
he crossed a deep body of water by boat that was over three hundred paces wide.
Traveling further southwest for sixty *li*,
one arrives at the city of Gandhāra. There,
two hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [a certain event occurred].
The Kaniṣka Stūpa, constructed by King Kaniṣka, consists of twelve tiers;
it stands seven hundred feet above the ground,
with a base over three hundred paces in width.
The steps were all made of patterned stone.
Within the stupa, the Buddhist icons underwent a thousand transformations and ten thousand variations.
The golden platters shimmer brightly;
the jeweled bells chime in harmony.
A stupa from the Western Regions.
It was the foremost of all.
Continuing northwest,
he crossed a great body of water.
I arrived at the country of Cina-kara,
where there was a stone stupa containing the Buddha’s cranial bone and an inscription in Brahmi script written by the Buddha’s own hand.
In total, I remained in the country of Wu-chang for two years.
In the second year of the Zhengguang era, he returned to the capital.
